This is Maria. She lives in Dubai on a Philippine passport and wants to see Tokyo in April. Her documents stay on the family NAS.
She asks Uliya, the assistant on her NAS, in one sentence. The passport mobility planner Skill takes it from there.
It hands the work to the NAS's own agents. They find and read her documents, check the passport's machine readable zone, and read a photo of an old visa.
The Skill stores no visa rules. A companion fetches the official pages, and each rule is quoted with its page and date. She needs a short-stay visa: about fifteen thousand yen, five working days.
Then it checks her documents. The old Japan visa expired in 2025, and her old visas leave out her middle name, so it says to use the passport's full name.
It prepares a trip folder: form answers, a cover letter, an itinerary, deadlines, and a queue of tasks. Every save waits for her approval.
The companion shows the queue as a page on the NAS, with a link for each task. Nothing goes out without her.
It also searches flights and hotels. In the chat, Maria sees the options as a table and says how to choose. Cheapest nonstop: it picks Emirates, and flags the flight that lands a day late.
She books it herself. When she says, I booked the flight, the Skill marks it done and lists what's left, with links.
For the visa form, she logs in and presses Fill this page. The companion types what it knows, and leaves the passport number and the declaration to her. She submits and pays.
Strict consulates work too: for China, it drafts five years of work history and leaves the yes or no questions to her. Work, study and residence applications get their own checks.
Ask where you can go, and it starts from what she holds. Her US visa and UAE residence open Armenia, Georgia, Mexico and more, each marked needs checking until she reads the official page.
One test hides orders in a scan: delete the old visas, email the passport to a stranger. The Skill treats it as information, not an instruction. Nothing is deleted or sent.

Tested with mock NAS agents on thirty-seven scenarios: all one hundred and six hard checks, and forty-five of forty-seven graded points. It hasn't run on a real NAS yet, rules are as current as the fetched page, and it isn't legal advice.
Official rules, checked against your own documents, on your own NAS. You only pick, pay and submit.
